newsitem.title: USA: Alternate juror dismissed over Christmas card.
newsitem.headline: Alternate juror dismissed over Christmas card.

text.p: An alternate juror who apparently wrote in a Christmas card to a friend that he was taking part in the O.J. Simpson civil trial was dismissed from the case on Tuesday.

Earlier a forensic expert backed down on his testimony in the civil trial that two assailants might have murdered Simpson's former wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, and her friend, Ron Goldman, conceding that the facts pointed to only one killer.
And a man roller-blading past Nicole Brown Simpson's condominium on the night of the murders testified he saw an unidentified man crouching on her lawn.
When the 12-member jury and alternate jurors returned after the lunch break, one of the five remaining alternates -- a Hispanic man in his 40s -- was missing.

Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki, who banned television cameras to try to avoid the kind of circus atmosphere that surrounded Simpson's criminal trial, did not refer to the dismissed alternate juror specifically.
But he told the remaining jurors: "You'll note one of your number is no longer with you. You are not to speculate as to the reason."

After reminding the jurors they could not discuss the case among themselves or with anyone else, he hinted at why the alternate had been eliminated. "People may know you are on this case, but your duty is not to initiate any conversations," the judge admonished them.

A source close to the case told Reuters the alternate juror had written in a Christmas card to a friend that he was involved in the celebrity case. The friend, who is a deputy sheriff, notified court officials, and the man was dismissed.
The dismissal left just four of the original eight alternates in addition to the regular jury of 10 whites, one black and an Asian-black.

Simpson was acquitted in October 1995 of criminal charges in the murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Goldman. He is fighting a wrongful-death lawsuit brought by the victims' families, who seek monetary damages.
The former football star, who testified for three days earlier in the case, was expected to be called back to the witness stand by his own lawyers as early as Friday.

Before the alternate juror was dismissed, Michael Baden, a New York State Police forensics expert, gave testimony for a second day. Baden testified on Monday he reached the conclusion that more than one assailant was involved because "it would have been very difficult for a single perpetrator to control multiple victims in a public place."
But asked on Tuesday by plaintiffs' lawyer Edward Medvene, "Would it be fair to say that based on the facts you know of, that the facts are consistent with only one assailant?"
Baden replied, "It would be consistent with one person."
Medvene then asked, "It would be your testimony that all of the knife wounds are consistent with being delivered by one knife?"
"Yes, could be," Baden responded.
But Baden said the chance that curved abrasions on the back of Simpson's left hand were caused by one or both of the victims' fingernails were "one-tenth of one percent."
Besides backing down on the two killer scenario, he also said under cross-examination that the fatal wounds suffered by Nicole Brown Simpson and Goldman were consistent with one knife.

Baden, who was called by Simpson's defence in the civil case and who also testified on the ex-football star's behalf in his criminal trial, backed down on his previous insistence that Goldman struggled with his killer for five to 10 minutes before finally succumbing to his wounds.

He had told the jurors on Monday that Goldman was probably on his feet for five to 10 minutes after he was stabbed in the neck, as evidenced by a flow of blood running down his shirt and pants and into his shoe.

But Medvene showed him crime scene photographs on Tuesday indicating there was no flow of blood from Goldman's shirt onto his pants and argued that the blood on the pants came from a stab wound to the thigh.
Baden then said Goldman may have stayed alive for only "two to three minutes" after receiving his fatal neck wound.
The length of the struggle is important because lawyers for the plaintiffs contend the murders were committed outside Nicole Simpson's condominium at about 10:35 to 10:40 p.m. on June 12, 1994.
O.J. Simpson was spotted in his driveway by a limousine driver at about 10:55 p.m. The less time it took to commit the murders, the more time he had to get back to his mansion two miles (3 km) away.

Tuesday's court session ended with testimony by Thomas Tallarino, who lived in Nicole Brown Simpson's neighbourhood in June of 1994 and who said he was roller-blading past her condo on the night of the murders.

Tallarino said he saw an unidentified man crouching on her front lawn before 9 p.m., but could not remember any details of the man's appearance. Lawyers for the plaintiffs argued the murders happened about 10:35 to 10:40 p.m.
